strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis of why naive text conditioning fails for diffusion-based visual representations in control, supported by cross-attention visualizations (Fig. 3) that convincingly show grounding failures in simulated environments compared to real-world-like tasks.

The proposed ORCA method (learnable task prompts + dense visual prompts from a frozen vision encoder) is simple, well-motivated by the preceding analysis, and integrates cleanly into a behavior-cloning pipeline without requiring diffusion model fine-tuning.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across three standard benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit; 12 tasks total) with multiple task-agnostic (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and task-adaptive (Text-Simple/Caption, CoOp, TADP) baselines, showing consistent (if sometimes modest) improvements.

Useful ablations on prompt components, U-Net layer selection, and diffusion timestep, plus an efficiency comparison and qualitative rollout visualizations that add interpretability to the design choices.

The paper's framing—that conditions for control need per-frame, fine-grained visual grounding rather than global text descriptions—is a reasonable and potentially generalizable insight beyond this specific method.
weaknesses: There appears to be a numerical inconsistency between the main results (Table 1, ORCA: Reacher-easy 87.6, Mean 74.3) and the timestep ablation (Table 6, t=0 'Default': Reacher-easy 71.9, Mean 70.8), which should represent the same configuration; this raises concerns about experimental consistency/correctness that are not explained in the text.

Evaluation scale is limited: only 5, 5, and 2 tasks are used from DMC, MetaWorld, and Adroit respectively, with very few demonstrations (2-5) per task, and no real-robot validation, which limits confidence in generalization of the claimed state-of-the-art results.

The method incurs substantially higher inference latency (48ms vs. 11ms for VC-1, per Table 7) and more parameters, but the paper does not thoroughly discuss this efficiency-performance trade-off or its practical implications for real-time robotic control.

The core technical contribution (combining learnable soft prompts akin to CoOp with dense features from a separate frozen vision encoder as visual conditioning) is an incremental combination of existing ideas from the vision-language prompting literature (CoOp, TADP, SD4Match, EcoDepth) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Component ablations (Table 4) show that using task or visual prompts alone can sometimes underperform the no-condition baseline (e.g., task-prompt-only on Cheetah-run: 38.9 vs. baseline 43.4), and this divergent, task-dependent behavior is not deeply analyzed beyond a brief qualitative remark.

Reported standard deviations are often large relative to inter-method differences (e.g., Cheetah-run ±8.4, ±10.1), raising questions about the statistical robustness of the claimed improvements given only three seeds.

The claimed 'domain gap' explanation for text-condition failure is illustrated qualitatively on only two example tasks (Button-press vs. Cheetah-run) rather than being quantified systematically across the full task suite.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated empirical investigation into why naive text conditioning fails for diffusion-based visual representations in robotic control, supported by cross-attention visualizations (Fig. 3) that offer some mechanistic insight into the domain-gap hypothesis.
The proposed method (learnable task prompts + dense visual prompts) is simple and easy to implement, requiring no fine-tuning of the diffusion backbone.

Experiments span three standard benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit) covering 12 tasks, with consistent gains over the compared baselines and reasonable ablations on prompt components, layer selection, and diffusion timestep.
Additional analyses (efficiency comparison, qualitative rollouts, attention visualization of task/visual prompts across frames) add some transparency to the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a combination of already-established components—CoOp-style learnable text prompts and external vision-encoder features injected as tokens (similar in spirit to SD4Match/EcoDepth/TADP, all cited by the authors)—applied to a new domain (control) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Because visual prompts are derived directly from a frozen, pre-trained DINOv2 encoder, it is unclear how much of the reported improvement stems from the diffusion model's representation versus simply from injecting strong DINOv2 features into the pipeline. No ablation isolates the diffusion model's marginal contribution (e.g., DINOv2-only policy vs. DINOv2-as-visual-prompt-in-diffusion), which undermines the core claim that 'conditioning the diffusion model' is what drives the gains.

Missing comparisons to widely used, more directly relevant control-representation baselines mentioned in the related work (R3M, VIP, MVP); the empirical comparison is restricted to CLIP, VC-1, and SCR, plus generic vision-perception prompting baselines (CoOp/TADP) not designed for control, making the 'state-of-the-art' claim less convincing.

The case study motivating the approach (Fig. 3) is based on only two tasks (Button-press vs. Cheetah-run), which is a fairly anecdotal basis for the general claim that text conditioning fails due to cross-attention grounding failure; a broader quantitative analysis of grounding quality across more tasks would strengthen this central argument.

Evaluation scale is modest: only 2–5 demonstrations per task and 2–5 tasks per benchmark (12 tasks total), which, combined with relatively high variance in some results (e.g., Table 3 Adroit, Table 6 timestep ablation), raises concerns about the robustness/generality of the reported improvements.

The efficiency comparison (Table 7) shows the method is roughly 2–4x slower than VC-1/SCR at inference and introduces ~10M extra learnable parameters plus a frozen DINOv2 encoder; this practical overhead is reported but not substantively discussed as a limitation for real-world deployment.

Component ablation (Table 4) shows that the task prompt alone can hurt performance on some tasks (e.g., Cheetah-run drops from 43.4 to 38.9), which is not adequately explained and slightly undercuts the narrative that task prompts alone reliably improve grounding.

The method is only validated on Stable Diffusion v1.5; no experiments test generalization to other diffusion backbones/architectures (e.g., SDXL, DiT-based models), leaving open whether the findings are backbone-specific.

strengths: The paper provides a well-motivated empirical diagnosis of why naive text conditioning fails for robotic control, using cross-attention visualizations (Fig. 3) to show that VLM-generated captions are often poorly grounded to relevant image regions in simulated control scenes, unlike in natural-image segmentation tasks. This analysis is a genuine and useful contribution independent of the proposed method.

The proposed ORCA method (learnable task prompts + frame-wise visual prompts from a frozen vision encoder) is simple, lightweight to add on top of a frozen diffusion model, and clearly motivated by the preceding analysis.

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: 12 tasks across three standard benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit), with consistent gains over task-agnostic baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR) and adapted task-adaptive baselines from other vision domains (CoOp, TADP).

Thorough ablations are provided: component-wise ablation (task vs. visual prompts), layer selection, diffusion timestep selection, efficiency/parameter comparison, and additional analysis of <bos>/<eos> attention behavior in the appendix, which supports the design choices.

Qualitative visualizations (cross-attention maps across frames, per-episode success/failure comparisons) help substantiate the quantitative claims and make the mechanism of the method more interpretable.
weaknesses: The evaluation, while spanning three benchmarks, uses fairly small task subsets (5+5+2) and low demonstration counts (2-5 per task); several results have large standard deviations relative to the reported gains (e.g., Cheetah-run 50.0±8.4 vs. TADP 41.1±3.9, Reacher-easy component ablation differences within 1 std), which makes some individual-task improvements less statistically conclusive, though the aggregated mean trends are consistent.

The method is only evaluated with Stable Diffusion v1.5 and DINOv2 as the fixed visual backbone; no exploration of whether findings generalize to newer/larger diffusion backbones or alternative vision encoders is provided, limiting insight into the robustness of the approach across compute/model regimes.

All experiments are conducted in simulation; there is no real-robot validation, which is a common but real limitation on the practical applicability of the claimed "task-adaptive representation" benefits for actual deployment.

The efficiency comparison (Table 7) shows ORCA has ~2-4x the inference latency and more parameters than VC-1/SCR; this added cost is reported but not deeply discussed in the context of real-time control feasibility.

The core technical novelty is a combination of established ideas (CoOp-style learnable text prompts, external vision-encoder features as visual conditioning similar to SD4Match/EcoDepth) repurposed for the control domain; the contribution is more of a careful empirical adaptation and diagnosis than a fundamentally new mechanism, which is acceptable but should be weighed against the paper's framing as introducing a new conditioning paradigm.

Baselines such as CoOp and TADP are adapted from classification/segmentation settings without much justification for why these specific adaptations are the strongest possible competitors from that literature; a more recent control-specific diffusion baseline beyond SCR would strengthen the comparison.

strengths: Provides a clear, well-motivated empirical analysis of why naive text conditioning (successful in other vision tasks) fails for diffusion-based visual representations in robotic control, supported by intuitive cross-attention visualizations that convincingly show grounding failures on tasks like Cheetah-run vs. Button-press.

Proposes a simple, low-overhead method (learnable task prompts + dense visual prompts) that consistently improves over a wide set of baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR, Text-based conditions, CoOp, TADP) across 12 tasks spanning three distinct benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit).

Extensive ablation studies are provided, including component analysis (task vs. visual prompts), U-Net layer selection, diffusion timestep selection, choice of external vision encoder, and comparison against full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, RoboAdapter), which strengthens the credibility of the design choices.

Supplementary experiments broaden scope credibly: testing alternate diffusion backbones (SVD, SD3/DiT), evaluating on LIBERO-Long (including multi-task setting), and comparing to stronger frozen encoders (DINOv2, SigLIP, Theia), which help contextualize where the method does and does not generalize.
Reasonable transparency about limitations (U-Net-specific findings, DiT underperformance) and efficiency/parameter trade-offs are explicitly reported.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is an incremental combination of existing techniques from other domains (CoOp-style learnable prompts, TADP/textual-inversion-style visual conditioning, external dense vision-encoder features) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the primary contribution is empirical/analytical rather than algorithmic novelty.

Performance gains are inconsistent in magnitude across benchmarks: substantial on some DMC tasks (e.g., Cheetah-run, Walker-walk) but marginal on several MetaWorld tasks relative to CoOp/TADP (e.g., Assembly, Hammer, Drawer-open all near-saturated or within noise), raising questions about how much of the improvement is driven by the visual-prompt component (which relies on an external pretrained encoder like DINOv2) versus the diffusion conditioning itself.

Evaluation is restricted to simulated benchmarks with very few demonstrations (2–5) and no real-robot validation; generalizability of learned task prompts to truly unseen tasks (beyond the LIBERO multi-task addendum) is not thoroughly established, since a task prompt is learned per task and may implicitly require task identity.

Reported results are based on only three seeds with sizable standard deviations in several tables (e.g., Adroit results, fine-tuning comparison), which weakens confidence in some of the smaller reported gains.

The method's benefit is tied specifically to U-Net-based Stable Diffusion; the paper's own supplementary results show the approach underperforms or is not well-supported on DiT-based (SD3) and video diffusion (SVD) backbones, limiting the generality of the claimed insights to a narrowing set of legacy architectures as the field moves toward DiT/video-based generative backbones.

Ablation in the appendix (SD-VAE achieving competitive results without DINOv2) suggests the visual prompt's gains may not strongly depend on rich pretrained visual semantics, which is left relatively underexplored/underexplained despite being central to the method's design rationale.

strengths: The paper provides a well-motivated diagnostic study (cross-attention visualization) that convincingly shows why naive text conditioning fails for robotic control, offering a useful negative result and analysis that could inform future work.

The proposed method (learnable task prompts + dense visual prompts from an external encoder) is simple and requires no fine-tuning of the diffusion backbone, which is a practical advantage over full fine-tuning approaches like SCR.

Extensive empirical coverage: 12 tasks across three standard benchmarks (MetaWorld, DMC, Adroit), plus substantial supplementary experiments (different diffusion backbones, LIBERO-Long, vision-encoder ablation, timestep ablation, comparison to parameter-efficient fine-tuning, efficiency analysis).
Reasonably thorough set of baselines adapted from the visual-perception literature (CoOp, TADP) into the control setting, allowing direct comparison of conditioning strategies.
Ablations (component analysis, layer selection) and qualitative visualizations (attention maps across frames) support the claimed mechanism of the method to some degree.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing techniques (CoOp-style learnable soft prompts, dense visual-encoder features as prompts) already used in TADP/CoOp for vision tasks, applied to a new but conceptually straightforward domain; the core contribution is more of an application/engineering combination than a new mechanism.

Reported gains over the strongest baselines (CoOp, TADP, Text-Caption) are frequently small (often 1-3 points) and fall within or close to the reported standard deviations across only 3 seeds, raising doubts about statistical significance of the claimed state-of-the-art results (e.g., Table 1 MetaWorld/DMC margins, Table 2 Adroit).

The visual prompt relies on an external pretrained vision encoder (DINOv2), and the ablation in the appendix (Table C) shows that using the diffusion model's own VAE features without any external encoder achieves competitive results, weakening the claim that the diffusion model conditioning itself (as opposed to simply adding another pretrained visual representation) is doing the heavy lifting.

Task prompts are learned per-task from scratch during downstream training rather than being reusable/transferable across tasks, which somewhat undercuts the "task-adaptive, single-model" framing and behaves similarly to task-specific policy tuning; scalability/generalization to unseen tasks is not evaluated.
Efficiency cost is non-trivial (48ms latency vs 11ms for VC-1, per Table F), a ~4x increase that is not thoroughly discussed in the context of real-time robotic control requirements.

Evaluation is restricted to simulated benchmarks with very few demonstrations (2-5) and short task lists; the LIBERO-Long results in the appendix also show large variances, and broader manipulation/real-world validation is absent.
Some presentation issues, including a duplicated paragraph describing Fig. 6 in the main text, reduce polish and suggest limited proofreading.
Baseline implementations (e.g., TADP, CoOp adaptations) are not deeply justified as being optimally tuned for the control setting, leaving some uncertainty about whether comparisons are fully fair.

strengths: The paper poses a clear, well-motivated research question—how to effectively condition text-to-image diffusion models for robotic control—and provides a systematic empirical investigation (text prompts, cross-attention visualization) before arriving at the proposed method, which makes the narrative convincing and easy to follow.

The core empirical observation that naive text conditioning (even from a strong VLM like Gemini 2.5) can hurt performance in control tasks, supported by cross-attention visualizations showing failure to ground words like 'cheetah' or 'run', is an interesting and non-obvious finding that contrasts with prior work in other vision domains (e.g., VPD).

The proposed method (ORCA) is simple, lightweight (only ~10.6M learnable parameters), and achieves consistent improvements across all 12 tasks spanning three diverse benchmarks (DMC, MetaWorld, Adroit), rather than trading off performance on some tasks for gains on others, which is a meaningful practical advantage over task-agnostic baselines.

The experimental section is thorough: comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (CLIP, VC-1, SCR, CoOp, TADP), ablations on task/visual prompt components, layer selection, timestep selection, vision encoder choice, comparison to full fine-tuning/parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and additional results with alternative diffusion backbones (SVD, SD3) and on LIBERO-Long, which strengthens the empirical support for the claims.
Efficiency analysis (Table F) and discussion of parameter counts versus VC-1/SCR helps contextualize the practicality of the added components.

Qualitative visualizations (cross-attention maps, frame-wise trajectory comparisons) provide reasonable interpretability of what task and visual prompts are learning, supporting the paper's hypothesis about frame-sensitive, task-grounded conditioning.
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to relatively short-horizon, single-task simulated benchmarks with very few demonstrations (2-5 per task); while LIBERO-Long results are included in the appendix, the core claims rest mainly on MetaWorld/DMC/Adroit, and there is no real-robot validation, which limits confidence in broader applicability.

The gains, while consistent, are often modest in several tasks (e.g., DMC Finger-spin, MetaWorld Drawer-open/Hammer are saturated near ceiling for most methods), and the paper does not report statistical significance testing beyond standard deviations over 3 seeds, making it hard to assess whether some improvements are within noise.

The explanation for why text conditions fail (domain gap between web images and simulated control scenes) is plausible but not rigorously established; the case study in Fig. 3 is based on only two illustrative tasks (Button-press vs Cheetah-run), and a more systematic quantitative analysis of grounding quality across all tasks (e.g., correlating attention map quality with performance) would strengthen this central claim.

The additional comparisons with more recent, stronger backbones (SD3/DiT, SVD) show ORCA's underlying design choices (e.g., layer selection, U-Net-specific extraction) may not transfer well to newer architectures, which is acknowledged as a limitation but somewhat undercuts the generality of the proposed conditioning strategy.

The method's reliance on an additional frozen vision encoder (DINOv2) for visual prompts adds a dependency and extra computational/latency overhead (Table F shows ~4x higher latency than VC-1), which is not deeply analyzed in terms of the trade-off against simpler task-agnostic alternatives.

Learned task prompts are shared across all observations within a task and optimized via the BC objective per-task; the paper does not clarify how this scales when task identity is unknown at test time or when tasks must be inferred online, limiting practical deployment scenarios beyond the fixed benchmark setting.
